passage:
Kiran sat on the colony terrace after dinner, picking at a loose thread on the cushion. Bhupen, a friend from the next building, had come up to return a notebook, phone in hand, scrolling.
"Can I tell you something?" said Kiran. "I keep lying awake thinking I'll blank on the chemistry paper. Everyone else seems fine."
Bhupen looked up. Then Bhupen turned the phone face down on the step and said, "Blank how? Like the whole paper, or one question that throws you off?"
Kiran hadn't expected that. Words came slowly at first, then all together. Bhupen didn't give a list of tips. Bhupen just nodded and asked, "And then what happens in your head?"
When Kiran got to the stairs, the shoulders felt lighter.

qa.q: Where was Kiran sitting when telling Bhupen about the worry?
qa.a: On the colony terrace after dinner, picking at a loose thread on the cushion.

qa.q: What did Kiran feel when Bhupen put the phone face down and asked a follow-up?
qa.a: Surprise, then relief. The words came slowly and then all together, and the shoulders felt lighter afterwards.

qa.q: What did Bhupen choose to do that made the difference?
qa.a: Bhupen turned the phone face down and asked a follow-up question instead of handing over a list of tips.

qa.q: What might Bhupen have been thinking when Kiran said, "Can I tell you something?"
qa.a: That Kiran wanted to be listened to, not fixed, which is why Bhupen put the phone away and asked what happens in the head.

grounding: A teenager tells a friend a worry, and the friend puts the phone down and asks a follow-up, so the teenager feels heard.

passage:
"Can I tell you something?" Dhruv said, sitting down on the bench by the bus stop next to Shalini, a friend since Class Five.
"Sure." Shalini was texting, but quickly slid the phone into a pocket. "Go on."
"I'm scared I'll freeze at the audition for the school play. My hands go cold even thinking about it."
"Cold hands. Wait, is it the first line that scares you most?"
"Yeah. Just the first line. After that I think I'd be okay."
"Then that's a really specific thing. Tell me more about the first line."
Dhruv laughed shakily. "You didn't tell me what to do."
"Did you want me to?"
"No. I wanted you to ask that." Dhruv leaned back. "Thanks for the pocket thing."

qa.q: What is Dhruv scared of?
qa.a: Freezing at the audition for the school play, especially on the first line.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when saying "Thanks for the pocket thing"?
qa.a: Grateful and relieved. Dhruv noticed Shalini put the phone away and felt that mattered more than advice.

qa.q: What did Shalini do that made Dhruv feel heard?
qa.a: Shalini slid the phone into a pocket, asked a follow-up about the first line, and did not offer advice unless it was wanted.

qa.q: What is it like for Shalini to hear "You didn't tell me what to do"?
qa.a: It may be a small surprise. Shalini can see that listening and asking counted for more than solutions, so asking "Did you want me to?" was the right move.

grounding: A teenager tells a friend a worry, sees the friend put the phone away and ask a follow-up, and feels heard more than advised.

passage:
"Ira, beta, you're staring at your phone like it owes you money," said Reena aunty, sitting on the swing. "Let me tell you something. When I was fifteen, my family was moving from Shimla to Delhi, and I was terrified. New school, no friends. I told my friend Sheetal on our last walk. She was holding a book she loved, and she closed it. Put it down on the bench. And she said, 'What scares you most about it?'
Nobody else had asked me that. My parents said it would be fine. My teacher said I'd make friends. Sheetal just asked, and then listened.
I cried a bit, told her about the lunchroom, the bus, everything. She didn't fix anything. But I felt like I mattered. I still remember that book on the bench, forty years later."

qa.q: What did Sheetal do with her book?
qa.a: She closed it and put it down on the bench.

qa.q: How did young Reena feel when Sheetal asked what scared her most?
qa.a: She felt truly heard and that she mattered, since no one else had asked.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Reena aunty's story?
qa.a: Sheetal putting the book down and asking a real question, which let Reena share her fears and feel heard.

qa.q: How might Sheetal have felt listening to Reena's fears?
qa.a: She probably felt sad about her friend leaving, but cared enough to put her book aside and listen.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how a friend putting a book down and asking a follow-up question made her feel truly heard as a teenager.

passage: The school bus was packed and the driver had the radio blaring when Anand finally said it to Nitin. "I think I'm getting dropped from the hockey team." Nitin was scrolling through videos. Anand sighed and looked out the window. Then he noticed: Nitin had put his phone face-down on his knee. "Wait, what? Why do you think that?" Anand was surprised. "Coach moved me to the reserves for the last two matches. And he didn't say anything." "That's rough. Did you ask him?" "No. I'm scared he'll say yes." "Want to go together tomorrow before practice?" Anand stared at the phone on Nitin's knee. It stayed there until their stop. Nitin didn't have a magic answer. But getting off the bus, Anand felt lighter than he had all week.

qa.q: How many matches had Anand been moved to the reserves for?
qa.a: The last two matches.

qa.q: What did Anand feel when he noticed Nitin's phone was face-down?
qa.a: He felt surprised and then that he mattered, because Nitin had set aside his phone to really listen.

qa.q: What small step did Nitin offer?
qa.a: To go with Anand to talk to Coach before practice tomorrow.

qa.q: What would change if Nitin had kept scrolling?
qa.a: Anand might have felt ignored and kept the worry to himself, feeling more alone.

grounding: Shows a teenager sharing a worry and feeling truly heard when a friend puts his phone down and asks a follow-up question.

passage: At the colony park in Lucknow, Asif sat on the swings with Damini after tuition. Damini was texting. "My Nani keeps forgetting things," Asif said, without looking up. "Yesterday she called me by my father's name." Damini's thumbs stopped. She put her phone in her pocket. "That sounds scary. How are you feeling about it?" Asif looked at her. He'd told two other friends, and both had said, "Oh, old people forget," and gone back to their phones. "Scared," he said. "She taught me to read." "Does your family know?" "Ammi's taking her to the doctor on Saturday." Damini nodded. "Can I check on you after?" Asif felt his throat tighten. He nodded. They swung quietly until the streetlights came on.

qa.q: What did Nani call Asif yesterday?
qa.a: By his father's name.

qa.q: How did Asif feel when Damini put her phone away?
qa.a: He felt surprised and truly heard, since his other friends had brushed it off, and his throat tightened with feeling.

qa.q: What did Damini do that made Asif feel he mattered?
qa.a: She stopped texting, put her phone away, and asked how he was feeling, then offered to check on him after Saturday.

qa.q: How might Damini have felt listening to Asif?
qa.a: She probably felt concerned for him and caring, which is why she offered to check in.

grounding: Shows a teenager sharing a worry and feeling he matters when a friend puts her phone away and asks a follow-up question.

passage:
"Ganga, can I tell you something weird?"
"Mm-hm." Her thumb kept scrolling.
"My Abbu might be moving to Muscat for work. For two years."
Ganga's thumb stopped. She put the phone face down on the bench.
"Wait. When did you find out?"
"Last night. I heard them talking. They don't know I know."
"How are you feeling about it? Honestly."
Rafiq opened his mouth to say "fine", and instead said, "Scared. He's the one who picks me up from cricket. Everything."
"That's a lot to carry since last night." She didn't offer a fix. She just waited.
He let out a long breath. "Yeah. Thanks for putting your phone down."
"It can wait. Tell me the rest."

qa.q: Where might Rafiq's Abbu move for work?
qa.a: He might move to Muscat, for two years.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel when Ganga put her phone face down?
qa.a: He felt noticed and relieved, safe enough to admit he was scared instead of saying fine.

qa.q: What did Ganga do that helped most?
qa.a: She put her phone away, asked how he honestly felt, and then waited instead of offering a fix.

qa.q: What would change if Ganga had kept scrolling?
qa.a: Rafiq would probably have said "fine" and kept the fear to himself, feeling he didn't matter much to her.

grounding: Shows a teenager sharing a worry and feeling truly heard when a friend puts her phone down and asks a follow-up question.
